founded.what: The year Nicolas Feuillatte launched the brand; the growers' co-operative union at Chouilly that has made it since 1986 was set up in 1972.

kind.means: A coopérative de manipulation: a co-operative that makes and sells wine from its members' grapes. Here it is a union of growers' co-operatives at Chouilly, and its labels carry the letters CM.

story: In 1972 the Centre Vinicole de la Champagne was set up at Chouilly, in the Côte des Blancs, as a union of growers' co-operatives, to help its growers sell their surplus grapes, by the house's account. In 1976 Nicolas Feuillatte, a businessman who had invested in Champagne vineyards at the age of forty, began selling a Champagne under his own name, first, by the house's own account, to a circle of American friends. In 1986 he passed the brand to the Centre Vinicole, which took the name Centre Vinicole Champagne Nicolas Feuillatte and has made the wine at Chouilly ever since. The prestige cuvée, Palmes d'Or, began with the 1985 vintage. The brand's founder died in August 2014, aged 88. The house calls itself the youngest of the Champagne houses: its growers own the vines, and the union presses, blends and ages their fruit. At the end of 2021 the union merged with the Coopérative Régionale des Vins de Champagne, the co-operative behind Castelnau, to form Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne, after both general assemblies voted for it on 15 December 2021. Nicolas Feuillatte and Castelnau went on as brands of their own within the new group, and in the autumn of 2023 the group completed its purchase of Champagne Henriot, of Reims.

style.line: Fresh, fruity and approachable, built on Pinot Noir and Meunier: the fruit of member growers across the appellation, blended and aged at Chouilly.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir and Meunier lead the non vintage Brut, 40 per cent each with 20 per cent Chardonnay, by the house; the members' vineyards spread across the appellation.
style.reserve: Reserve wines go into the non vintage blends, chosen, in the house's words, for their quality, consistency, diversity and ageing potential; it gives no share.
style.vessels: Temperature controlled stainless steel tanks for Palmes d'Or, by the importer's and a merchant's accounts; no house page read names the vessels.
style.lees: Réserve Exclusive Brut ages three to four years in the cellars, and the Palmes d'Or range at least ten years, by the house.

nv.name: Réserve Exclusive Brut
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, Pinot Noir and Meunier leading with a fifth of Chardonnay, aged three to four years: the bottle most guests already know.

cuvee.name: Palmes d'Or

first.what: The first vintage, by a critic's vertical tasting and a merchant's listing of the 1985.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only as a vintage wine, in the years the house chooses, from the 1985 on: the 1990, 1995, 1998, 2002, 2008 and 2009 are among the vintages sold.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alone, in equal parts by the house's page for the 2008; accounts of the first, the 1985, differ over which grape led.
cuvee.sites: Nearly all Grand Cru, by the house. For the 2009 its notes name Chardonnay of Avize, Oger, Cramant and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Pinot Noir of Ambonnay and Verzenay, and the house adds Chardonnay of Montgueux, in the Aube.
cuvee.making: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, nearly all Grand Cru, made in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks by the importer's account. The wine then ages on its lees at Chouilly for at least ten years before release, by the house. The dosage is set for each release, and no figure in grams was found.
cuvee.lees: At least ten years in the cellars at Chouilly, by the house's own pages for the Palmes d'Or range.
cuvee.bottle: A black, opaque bottle made for this cuvée alone, faceted like a precious stone in the house's own words: the dimpled black glass by which a candidate knows it.
cuvee.young: Dried almond, apricot and fresh white fruit on the nose, then toffee, lemon curd and brioche on the palate, as critics describe it on release.
cuvee.aged: Older vintages turn to fine pastry and caramel, with touches of fennel, star anise and lemon peel and a full, silky texture, in notes of the 1990 and the 1995.

forms.name: Palmes d'Or Rosé
forms.note: Palmes d'Or Rosé Intense: Pinot Noir alone, from Grand Cru Bouzy and from Les Riceys, made by saignée, by the house.

forms.name: Chronothèque Palmes d'Or
forms.note: Late releases of old vintages, the 1999, 2000 and 2002, kept more than twenty years in the cellars before release, by the house.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

table.house45: Nicolas Feuillatte is the Champagne of a union of growers' co-operatives at Chouilly, in the Côte des Blancs. The union was set up in 1972 to help growers sell their surplus grapes. In 1976 Nicolas Feuillatte, a businessman who had invested in Champagne vineyards, launched a Champagne under his own name. In 1986 he passed the brand to the union, so every bottle comes from the grapes of member growers. The style is fresh and fruity, led by Pinot Noir and Meunier, and Réserve Exclusive Brut is the bottle guests know. Palmes d'Or, in its black bottle, is the prestige cuvée.
table.house10: Nicolas Feuillatte is the brand of a growers' co-operative union at Chouilly, launched by one man in 1976 and passed to the union in 1986.
table.cuvee45: Palmes d'Or has been Nicolas Feuillatte's prestige cuvée since the 1985 vintage, made only as a vintage wine. It is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in equal parts, nearly all from Grand Cru villages such as Verzenay, Cramant and Avize. It rests at least ten years in the cellars at Chouilly before release. You will know it by its black bottle, faceted like a precious stone. Dried almond, apricot and brioche come through, with a note of lemon curd. A tulip or a white wine glass at 8 to 10 degrees suits it.
table.sale: Palmes d'Or is a prestige Champagne from the growers' own grapes, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, nearly all Grand Cru and aged at least ten years. Shall I bring a bottle in its black glass?
table.cuvee10: Palmes d'Or is the vintage prestige cuvée of Nicolas Feuillatte, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in a black, faceted bottle.
table.cuvee20: Nicolas Feuillatte first made Palmes d'Or with the 1985 vintage. It is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in equal parts, nearly all Grand Cru, aged at least ten years at Chouilly.

guests.q: Was Nicolas Feuillatte a real person?
guests.a: Yes. He launched the brand in 1976 and in 1986 passed it to the union of growers' co-operatives at Chouilly, which has made the wine since. He died in 2014, aged 88.
Not in the strict sense. It is co-operative Champagne: thousands of growers pool their grapes and the union makes the wine, where a grower Champagne is one family bottling its own vines.
The house made the black, opaque bottle for Palmes d'Or alone, faceted like a precious stone in its own words, so it stands apart from the usual green glass.
No. It is a Brut, so dry, with the dosage set for each release; the richness comes from Pinot Noir and ten years in the cellar.

traps: The class sheet prints Cuvée Palms d'Or; the label and the house's own pages read Palmes d'Or, with an e, French for golden palms.
Nicolas Feuillatte was a real man who launched the brand in 1976, but since 1986 it has been the brand of a growers' cooperative group.
Cooperative Champagne is not grower Champagne: many growers pool their grapes, rather than one family bottling its own vines.
Palmes d'Or is Nicolas Feuillatte's, in the black faceted bottle; Belle Epoque is Perrier-Jouët's, in the bottle painted with anemones.

sheet.note: The sheet writes Palms for Palmes and adds Cuvée. The house's own pages name the wine Palmes d'Or, the golden palms; some merchants' listings of older vintages add Cuvée, which the sheet may follow.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée of the class sheet comes from the union of growers' co-operatives at Chouilly?
questions.exp: Palmes d'Or is Nicolas Feuillatte's, made by the co-operative union at Chouilly. Belle Epoque is Perrier-Jouët's, Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's and Celebris is Gosset's.

questions.q: In which year did Nicolas Feuillatte pass his brand to the co-operative union at Chouilly?
questions.exp: He passed the brand to the union in 1986. The union was set up in 1972, he launched the brand in 1976, and in 2021 the union merged into Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne.

questions.q: Which vintage is given as the first Palmes d'Or, the prestige cuvée of Nicolas Feuillatte?
questions.exp: Palmes d'Or began with the 1985 vintage. 1976 is the year the brand was launched, 1972 the year the union was set up, and 1999 one of the old vintages of the Chronothèque.

report: Built on the library's p-nicolas-feuillatte, contradicting it in one figure: the library says Palmes d'Or ages at least nine years, the house's pages say at least ten for the Palmes d'Or range, which this record follows; listed for the owner.
founded.year is the library's brand year, 1976; the library's 1972 for the co-operative is told in founded.what and the story.

kind.code CM was read from a label's traceability code (CM 815 001 on a Brut Réserve in Open Food Facts) and a wine guide calls the house a coopérative de manipulation; a refuter should read a label of Palmes d'Or itself.

Nicolas Feuillatte's dates: he died in August 2014 aged 88 by the Drinks Business and Decanter (one Decanter piece says 89); no birth year was found in two sources, so the plan's 1926 is not given and he is dated by his death.

The founder of the Centre Vinicole in 1972 is named on the house's own pages and is described, not named, since his dates were not found; the refuter cut the family vineyard at Bouleuse, since the house says Nicolas Feuillatte invested in Champagne vineyards at forty and one account has the house buying the Bouleuse vineyard.

The merger: both assemblies voted on 15 December 2021 and it took effect at the end of 2021, by Decanter and the Drinks Business, though some reports say 1 January 2022; the group's purchase of Champagne Henriot is told as the Henriot record's refuter dated it, completed in the autumn of 2023 (signed on 29 September, announced in October), so the two records agree; added by the integrator.

The first vintage 1985 rests on Wine Spectator's vertical and an Idealwine listing; they disagree on the 1985's blend (three fifths Chardonnay against three fifths Pinot Noir), so the record says accounts differ.

Vessels: stainless steel tanks for Palmes d'Or by Palm Bay and a Swiss merchant's listing of the 2008; style.malolactic and style.dosage are empty, since no page read gives either, and no dosage in grams was found for Palmes d'Or.

The glass: the young notes are critics' notes of the 2008 reproduced by a merchant (wine.com), the aged notes those of the 1990 and 1995 on the same merchant's pages; the house's own notes were not read.
The villages are the house's notes of the 2009; the share of Grand Cru, nearly 95 per cent, is the house's for the 2008.
The library's shared traps are kept word for word, its spelling cooperative and its present tense included, because a shared trap must read alike; the record's own prose writes co-operative.
The serving temperature is the Codex's reference for sparkling wine; the house's own figure was not found.
